clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in GABRA1, encoding the alpha-1 subunit of the GABA-A receptor, the principal fast inhibitory chloride-conducting ligand-gated channel of the brain.

The phenotype is a continuum: inherited variants tend to cause milder genetic generalised epilepsies such as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and childhood absence epilepsy, whereas de novo variants cause severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.
Severe cases resemble other early-infantile encephalopathies, including West syndrome (infantile spasms), Ohtahara syndrome and a Dravet-like course.
Seizure types are varied — myoclonic, absence, focal, tonic-clonic and spasms — with developmental slowing or regression at the encephalopathic end of the spectrum.
It is one of several GABA-A receptor subunit epilepsies, and identifying the specific gene requires panel or exome testing.
Loss-of-function or dominant-negative variants reduce GABAergic inhibition, tipping cortical networks towards hyperexcitability.
Management uses broad-spectrum antiseizure medicines; agents that potentiate GABA-A signalling are often chosen, though response is variable.
reference.pathophysiology: GABRA1 encodes the alpha-1 subunit of the pentameric GABA-A receptor, the most widely expressed alpha subunit, which forms the ligand-gated chloride channel mediating fast inhibitory neurotransmission. Pathogenic variants — frequently de novo missense or truncating changes — reduce surface receptor expression or channel function through loss-of-function or dominant-negative mechanisms, diminishing inhibitory tone and promoting neuronal network hyperexcitability and seizures. The severity gradient broadly parallels the degree of functional impairment, so that near-complete loss produces developmental and epileptic encephalopathy while partial dysfunction yields milder generalised epilepsy. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, with the severe encephalopathic cases usually arising de novo.
additionalDifferentials: Other GABA-A receptor subunit encephalopathies (GABRB3, GABRB2, GABRG2, GABRA5, GABRD)
Structural or metabolic causes of infantile epileptic encephalopathy
additionalInvestigations: Epilepsy gene panel or trio exome/genome sequencing
EEG, which may show generalised spike-wave, hypsarrhythmia, burst-suppression or multifocal discharges depending on phenotype
Brain MRI, usually normal or nonspecific
Metabolic screen to exclude treatable mimics
Parental testing to establish de novo status or inheritance
redFlags: Onset of intractable seizures in early infancy with developmental arrest
Status epilepticus or seizure clustering with febrile illness
reference.prognosis: Outcome is wide-ranging: inherited generalised epilepsy phenotypes may be well controlled with preserved cognition, whereas de novo encephalopathic cases often have refractory seizures with moderate-to-severe intellectual disability.
pitfalls: Assuming a single gene from the phenotype alone, since the GABA-A subunit epilepsies overlap clinically and require genetic testing.
Overlooking milder familial generalised epilepsy caused by the same gene.
Expecting a diagnostic MRI, as imaging is usually unremarkable.
Assuming that GABAergic agents will always help, since response is variable despite the mechanism.
management: Seizure control with antiseizure medications tailored to the phenotype, using broad-spectrum agents such as valproate, levetiracetam or lamotrigine for the generalised epilepsies and ethosuximide for absences

For the encephalopathic and infantile-spasm phenotypes, hormonal therapy with corticotrophin or corticosteroids or treatment with vigabatrin, and consideration of the ketogenic diet in drug-resistant seizures
Early developmental intervention with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy for the associated developmental delay or regression
Serial EEG and developmental or neuropsychological surveillance to guide treatment
Genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant disorder, with parental testing to establish de novo status and define recurrence risk
Multidisciplinary care led by paediatric neurology and epileptology
